5-1142 DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR UNITED STATES INDIAN SERVICE Colville Agency, Nespelem, Wash., July 1, 1919. Superintendent E. H. Hammond, Cushman Indian School, Tacoma, Wash. Dear Mr. Hammond: You failed to enclose copy of the correspondence you had with reference to the trio, who were guilty of check raising. Your letter, however, contains sufficient information. Since the girls agree to remain in school until excused by the banker, I am of the opinion that they should remain with you during the vacation, otherwise they will be getting off too easy. I respectfully suggest that you write the parents of Mary James and Collette Martin, advising them that the girls are contented, well and getting along very nicely. This will have a tendency to put them at ease. Then perhaps they will cease bombarding you with requests for the girls to return for the vacation. I will leave the matter wholly to your judgement. Yours very truly, Fred C. Morgan Superintendent FCM:MG For Collette, Mary Martin - Keller, Wash. Houser COLVILLE AGENCY RECEIVED JUL 2, 1919 5-1142 DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR UNITED STATES INDIAN SERVICE Colville Agency, Nespelem, Wash., June 30, 1919. Supt. E. L. Hammond, Cushman Indian School, Tacoma, Wash. Dear Mr. Hammond: The parents of Mary James and Colette Martin desire to learn whether or not their daughters will be permitted to return home for the summer vacation. Mrs. James appears to be particularly interested in having Mary home for the purpose of assisting her in farming operations. I realize that these girls got in bad on account of the forged checks. However, I do not recall that you advised me just what punishment was meted out to them. Please advise me in order that I may tell their parents, who have been very anxious to learn whether or not they will come home this summer. Very truly yours, Fred C. Morgan Superintendent. FCM:MJ Cushman Indian School Tacoma, Wash., July 28, 1919 Dear Mrs. James: I wrote to Mr. Morgan telling why Mary did not return home for the vacation. I did not punish her for running away. The banker told the girls that he would not prosecute them if they promised to remain in school until he excused them or until they had finished their course. Mary appears to be contented. She is certainly very well and is getting along nicely. She was promoted to Grade VI and tells me she is very glad she returned to school although during the vacation she is sometimes lonesome when the other girls are out picking berries. Mary went one day, but does not like it as it is too hot for her. I will take good care of Mary's health and will do all I can to keep her well and happy. Very sincerely yours, Superintendent. EHH:MG Mrs. Sarah James, Keller, Wash. Dr. Henry James: I received your letter of June 22nd asking for Mary's return for the vacation period. When she came back to school, the president of the Sumner State Bank promised not to prosecute her for raising the check provided she stayed in school returned the full amount of fifty dollars and remained in school until he gave her permission to go home. You need not feel sorry for Mary at all. Of course, she would prefer to spend her vacation at home but she is not unhappy except when your letters make her homesick. She has been a good girl and I feel sure will be reaping the benefits by remaining at school until next June. Sincerely yours, Keller Washington June 25th 1919 Dear Agency, I thought of writing to you just a little about my girl. Will you please send my daughter back soon and again having hard time lonely for her. So please send her back till school takes up again. I will send her back to school. I am so sorry for her if you don't send her back. Then I'll not anybody to take care of my some times. You've hard time when I get sick. I am having heart troubles. If I had a man's son, I would have somebody to take care of me. It would be alright for her to stay there at school. But I am all alone. And I am old now. Yours Respectfully, Mrs Sarah Jones Write soon and let me know please. THE FIRST NATIONAL BANK OF HOQUIAM W.L. ADAMS, PRESIDENT A.G. Inasmuch as we have received the $50.00 we are returning check #932 herewith. Yours respectfully, A.G. Rockwell Cashier. AGR:FR Cushman Indian School Tacoma, Washington February 17, 1919. Kindly read this letter to them and advise us as to whether they thoroughly agree to the above. Yours respectfully, The First National Bank of Hoquiam, Washington By [signature] A. G. DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR UNITED STATES INDIAN SERVICE COLVILLE AGENCY, NESPELEM, WASH. January 16, 1919. Mr. E. H. Hammond, Supt. Cushman Indian School, Tocoma, Washington. Dear Mr. Hammond: Reference is made to your telegram of January 15, 1919, (Mary James and Colett Martin raised and cashed check unless they return and settle this bank at once, charge of forgery and altering check will be made by bank). I at once sent for the girls. Mary James has just left the office, she stated that Viola Reynolds conceived the idea of raising the check referred to in your telegram and advised her, Mary, to do so. Mary states that she altered the check by adding a cipher to the figure (5), and adding the letter (y) to the word five, making it read Fifty dollars and no/100, ($50.00). Mary further states that Viola forged Mary's name in endorsing the check, that she, Viola, cashed the check and gave Mary $5.00 keeping $45.00 to cover the expenses of herself and Mary Iswald to Wenatchee. The only part that I can learn that Colett Martin took in the matter was that she advised Mary to raise the check, stating that it could be done and they would not be caught. I have not been able to see Colett, but as soon as I have had an interview with her I will write you again. Mary James has agreed to return to Cushman and explain the entire transaction, of course I advised her to do this, telling her it was my opinion that if she were truthful in the matter that you would assist her in having the matter properly adjusted with bank officials. Very respectfully, Fred C. Morgan Superintendent. THE FIRST NATIONAL BANK OF HOQUIAM W. L. ADAMS, President A. G. ROCKWELL, Cashier CAPITAL $100,000.00 SURPLUS $150,000.00 HOQUIAM, WASH. January 18, 1919 Ernest H. Hammond, Superintendent Cushman Indian School Tacoma, Washington Dear Sir: We have your letter of January 16th regarding the check of $5.00 payable to Mary James which had been raised. We are quite relieved to have the information given us in your letter and will be pleased to have our money as soon as convenient to send it. It might be a great help to us if the Government would see fit to install a protectograph in your office as it would eliminate all dangers of checks being raised or changed in any way. Yours very truly, The First National Bank of Hoquiam By (Mrs.) Iarna Reynolds Auditing Department IR:FR CUSHMAN INDIAN SCHOOL, TACOMA, WASH. January 15, 1919. I, Viola Runnels, do hereby voluntarily make the following statements which are true to the best of my knowledge. We, (Nancy & Mary James, Mary Iswald, Colette Martin and myself) were up in the dormitory. We were going to run away Sunday night but didn't get away until Monday morning, October 2d. Mary James said that she never had enough money and didn't know what she could do with a check for only $5. Then she said; "Let us change it into $50." I said: "Would we get caught?" and she said: "No, because I will change my name different and we won't get caught." She then wanted to know what we would do and I told her we would do anything that you will and so did Mary Iswald. Then she said, "How will we rub the $5. and make it $50. I can put the naught right by the five and make it fifty." I told her it was all right and she asked Mary Iswald, and she told her the same. Then she took a knife and scraped the "e" in five and changed it to fifty. Then she changed the name on the check to Margaret Jameson and signed it on the back that way. I went downstairs then but the check was fixed before I went away. The morning we ran away, we went out the end of the grounds and Mary James led the way around the streets until we came to the Puyallup road then we took a bus and got to Puyallup. We didn't know where we wanted to go but finally we took another bus to Sumner. When we got to Sumner we asked the way to the depot and Mary James asked me to take the check in and get it cashed. When I asked the agent to cash the check he asked me how much it was for and I told him fifty dollars. He said he couldn't cash such a large check. Mary James had some silver and greenbacks besides the check and when I couldn't get it cashed she said we would go to get something to eat and then buy some hats. She and I wanted to buy a hat. When we got through eating, we went to buy the hats and after we had them picked out, she didn't have enough money to pay for my hat so I took the check to buy the hat with. The lady asked us whose check it was and I said it was Mary James. Then Mary James paid the lady for my hat and took the money herself. She gave me $10 and she gave Mary Iswald $10, but when we got outside again, she took my $10 and said I might lose it. Mary Iswald did not have anything to do with the raising of the check but she was present when the check was cashed and shared in the sum of $10. When Mary James divided the money, she said "Now if we get caught, you will each have to pay $10." Viola Runnels Cushman Indian School, Tacoma, Wash. Jan. 16, 1919. The First National Bank, Bellingham, Washington. My Dear Mr. Reynolds: I am returning herewith the check for five ($5.00) dollars raised to fifty ($50.00). There is no doubt that Mary James raised the check, or aided and abetted in raising the check and received and distributed the money. She ran away from school telling one of her friends that if "they" found out about the check, "they" would give her the "dickens". She is at Keller, Washington. I have written her superintendent and there will be no trouble in having the money refunded immediately. If Mary alone were implicated, I would let her take her medicine, but there is a minor, who did not realize the seriousness of the offense until it was pointed out to her. If the refund of the money is satisfactory, it will be made through her Superintendent. Very truly yours, Superintendent THE FIRST NATIONAL BANK OF HOQUIAM W. L. ADAMS, PRESIDENT A. G. ROCKWELL, CASHIER CAPITAL $100,000.00 SURPLUS $150,000.00 HOQUIAM, WASH. January 13, 1919 Ernest Hammond, Superintendent Cushman Indian School Tacoma, Washington Dear Sir: We have your letter of January 10th regarding a check numbered 932 issued to Mary James in the sum of $5.00. We hand you herewith this cancelled check for your inspection. After receiving your letter, we inspected the check and immediately noticed that the name of the payee had been changed and that the amount had been raised to $50.00. This was not noticed at the time the check was cashed. We are sending the check to you thinking that you might have some idea as to who changed it. The endorsement on the back is undoubtedly a forgery. Would it be possible for you to find out whether or not this writing is that of Mary James? We will credit your account $45.00 to cover this check and will change the amount of it on our statement to read $5.00 instead of $50.00. After you have inspected the check kindly return it to us, at your earliest convenience, and we will endeavor to collect our money from the bank who originally cashed it. Yours very truly, Isma Reynolds Auditing Department I ENCLS IR:FR Govt. Day Western Union Superintendent Morgan Hespelem, Washington, Telephone from Wilbur Tacoma, Washington, Jan. 15, 1919 Hammond Mary James and Collete Martin raised and cashed check. Unless they return and settle with bank at once, charge of forging and uttering check will be made by bank. Cushman Indian School Confirmation of phone message Cushman Indian School, Tacoma, Wash. Jan. 15, 1919. Capt. Fred C. Morgan, Colville Agency, Nespelem, Wash. My Dear Mr. Morgan: Enclosed please find statement by Viola Runnels regarding the forging and uttering check. The check was originally for $5.00. It was raised by Mary James to $50.00 and the money distributed among Mary James, Mary Iswald, Colette Martin, and Viola Runnels. It wouldn't surprise me to learn that Mary James and Viola Runnels planned the scheme and carried it through successfully. The others are guilty to the extent of profiting by their cuteness. I don't want those two girls here. They are too "smart", but I can't think of any other way to save Mary Iswald who received and spent $10.00 of the funds and who was led on by the more cunning Mary James and Viola Runnels. Very respectfully, Superintendent VACATION REQUEST FOR PUPIL. We, the undersigned, respectfully request that leave of absence be granted ____________________________ from June 15, 1918 to Sept. 5, 1918 to enable ___________ to visit __________ home. We hereby agree to pay all expenses, including round-trip railroad fares, sleeping-car fares, meals, lodging, stage fares, telegraph and telephone messages, and other incidental expenses connected with the visit. We further agree that said pupil shall be returned to the Cushenaw school on or before the last day of the leave of absence. We further agree to deposit with the superintendent of the school sufficient money to defray all expenses to be incurred, and should the pupils, or any one of them, fail to return to school at such time as may be agreed upon by the parents or guardian and the superintendent of the school in which the pupils are enrolled, the amount of money remaining with the superintendent, necessary to the return transportation of the pupil or pupils so neglecting to return, shall be forfeited to the Government; provided, however, that in all cases where it can be shown that there were justifiable reasons for the failure of the return of the pupil the forfeiture of the funds shall not take place. If the pupil neglecting to return is from a reservation, the superintendent of the reservation shall certify to the reasons for the nonreturn of the pupil or pupils. If a pupil's home is not on a reservation, then the certificate of some reputable, disinterested citizen of the community may be requested as to the reasons for the nonreturn of the pupil or pupils. This form must be executed in duplicate when a child is transferred from a reservation to a nonreservation school. The Superintendent of the nonreservation school will retain the original for his files, and the duplicate shall be deposited in the reservation school records. The reservation superintendent should send to the Commissioner of Indian Affairs his certificate as provided by law. All the blanks must be properly filled in every case. If the information called for on any part of the blank is not known, that fact should be stated. No space should be left unfilled. Whether the parents are living or dead, their names must be given. The person who signs the blank as consenting to the transfer should indicate his relation to the applicant by marking out the word "parent," "guardian," or "next of kin," leaving unmarked only the title appropriate to the signer. INDORSEMENTS. The laws relating to the transfer of Indian children from reservations and schools are as follows: That hereafter no Indian child shall be sent from any Indian reservation to a school beyond the State or Territory in which said reservation is situated without the voluntary consent of the father or mother of such child if either of them are living, and if neither of them are living without the voluntary consent of the next of kin of such child. Such consent shall be made before the agent of the reservation, and he shall send to the Commissioner of Indian Affairs his certificate that such consent has been voluntarily given before such child shall be removed from such reservation. And it shall be unlawful for any Indian agent or other employee of the Government to induce, or seek to induce, by withholding rations or by other improper means, the parents or next of kin of any Indian to consent to the removal of any Indian child beyond the limits of any reservation. (28 Stats., p. 906.) Provided, That hereafter no Indian child shall be taken from any school in any State or Territory to a school in any other State against its will or without the written consent of its parents. (29 Stats., p. 348.) That no Indian pupil under the age of fourteen years shall be transported at Government expense to any Indian school beyond the limits of the State or Territory in which the parents of such child reside or of the adjoining State or Territory. (35 Stat. L., 781.) The rules provide that— A pupil who has been regularly enrolled in a nonreservation school must not be taken to any other nonreservation school without the consent of both superintendents and the Commissioner of Indian Affairs, and superintendents will be held to strict accountability for such pupils taken to their schools. An Indian boy or girl 18 years old and over may, without the consent of parents or others, personally sign the application form on its being changed to suit the case; but in all cases where the parents are living they should first be consulted. This form is to be used only in transfers from reservations or Indian schools to nonreservation schools.
